title: Acknowledgment
Exploration Optimization for Dynamic Assortment Personalization under Linear Preferences
authors: Fernando G. Bernstein; Sajad Modaresi; Denis Saure
affiliations: Duke University, The Fuqua School of Business, Durham, North Carolina, United States; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Kenan-Flagler Business School, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States; University of Chile, Industrial Engineering, Santiago, Chile
abstract: We study dynamic assortment personalization, where an online retailer adaptively selects assortments based on customer attributes to learn preferences and maximize revenue. We assume that product utilities depend linearly on customer attributes through an unknown coefficient matrix, leading to an exploration–exploitation trade-off. We identify price-driven and linearity-driven exploration efficiencies, showing that not all products need to be offered to all customer profiles to recover optimal assortments. We establish an instance-dependent regret lower bound characterized by a linear program, which we call the Regret Lower Bound (RLB) problem. Because the RLB has a complex structure and depends non-trivially on unknown parameters, we introduce an alternative formulation, called the Exploration-Optimization problem, that yields an interpretable exploration structure and can be formulated as a tractable mixed-integer linear program. We develop learning policies that select efficient exploration sets by solving either problem and establish a regret upper bound for the Exploration-Optimization policy. Using data from a large Chilean retailer, we demonstrate that our policies substantially outperform Thompson sampling in terms of both regret and computational efficiency, while remaining scalable in practice.

title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
authors: Sumit Agarwal; Johan Sulaeman; Yue Zhang; Zhe Zong
affiliations: NUS Business School and Sustainable and Green Finance Institute (SGFIN), National University of Singapore, 119245, Singapore; International School of Business & Finance and Advanced Institute of Finance, Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai 519082, China; China Zheshang Bank, Hangzhou 310020, China
abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
authors: Sevgi Soylemezgil; Cihan Uzmanoglu
affiliations: Binghamton University, Binghamton, New York 13902
abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
authors: Ming Hu; Chaoyu Zhang
affiliations: Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 3E6, Canada; College of Business, City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon, Hong Kong
abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use our theory model prediction as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using our model predictor, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. title: Advertising by Recruiting Influencers
authors: Maya Jalloul; Vasiliki Kostami
affiliations: Paris School of Business, 75005 Paris, France; HEC Paris, 78351 Jouy-en-Josas, France
abstract: The rise of social media platforms has enabled customers to rely on influencers and peer reviews to guide their purchasing decisions. As products increasingly focus on experiences, firms are leveraging influencer marketing as a crucial tool. This paper addresses key challenges of influencer marketing by considering different types of influencers and partnership schemes alongside the impact of social learning. We introduce a two-period model wherein, in the initial period, the firm unveils a new product experience of unknown quality alongside an influencer marketing campaign. The campaign relies on two types of influencers that differ in popularity and engagement levels and two partnerships: sponsored advertising and public relations. Customers base their purchasing decisions on their original (heterogeneous) beliefs, influencer-driven information, and reviews from early adopters in the second period. When customers are equally likely to follow any given influencer, the firm should choose a single influencer type and partnership. Consumer reviews complement influencer marketing when products are initially undervalued, increasing the returns to influencer investment. Moreover, within a societal structure characterized by distinct classes, in which followers and influencers often belong to the same class, a mix of influencer types and partnership schemes may become optimal. Our study provides guidance on selecting influencer types, partnership schemes, and social media platforms based on engagement, popularity, audience composition, and platform characteristics. This paper was accepted by Jeanette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07919 .

title: Negotiating Competing Expectations—Chiefs and Mineral Governance in Ghana
authors: Joel Agbesinyale
affiliations: Department of Global Political Studies Malmö University Malmö Sweden
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines what shapes chiefs' discretionary decision‐making and how they exercise authority within hybrid governance arrangements, focusing on Ghana's artisanal and small‐scale mining (ASM) sector. Existing scholarship recognizes that traditional authorities can strengthen or undermine state governance but offers limited explanations for variation in their practices. Drawing on interviews with chiefs, miners, and state officials, the paper develops a discretionary governance framework that integrates hybrid governance, access theory, and discretion. It argues that overlapping customary and statutory authority creates a discretionary space for chiefs to navigate competing expectations. Chiefs exercise this discretion through diverse governance practices, including restricting access to mining sites, mobilizing communities, and collaborating with state institutions, as well as facilitating access to land, negotiating informal payments, and shielding unauthorised miners from enforcement. These practices can reinforce, negotiate, circumvent, or undermine formal mining regulation. The paper advances debates on traditional authority and hybrid governance while challenging assumptions that constitutionally empowering chiefs necessarily strengthens mineral governance.

title: Correction to “Institutional Backsliding Under Liberal Democratic Backsliding: Central Bank Independence Reversal in Türkiye”
One Meeting That Should Not Be an Email: Manager–Direct Report One‐on‐One Meetings and Employee Engagement
authors: Jon Gray; Jonathan Flinchum; Steven Rogelberg; Matthew J. Gerson; Nicholas J. Dilley; Liana Kreamer
affiliations: University of North Carolina Charlotte North Carolina USA; Florida Institute of Technology Melbourne Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Building and maintaining an engaged workforce is a priority for organizations worldwide. While the antecedents and benefits of an engaged workforce are well documented, organizations continue to struggle to keep employees engaged. These ongoing difficulties point to the need for alternative, practical ways to foster engagement at work. To this end, we examine whether workplace meetings, specifically one‐on‐one (1:1) meetings between managers and direct reports, can foster engagement. Grounded in job demands and resources (JD‐R) theory, self‐determination theory (SDT) and Kahn's engagement theory, we hypothesized that 1:1 meeting quantity and quality promote engagement by satisfying employees' basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. We tested a moderated mediation model using two time‐separated online surveys ( N = 303). Results indicated that meeting quality, reflected in a managers' task‐ and relations‐oriented behaviors in 1:1 s, was more consistently associated with engagement than meeting quantity. These relationships remained after accounting for managers' use of the same behaviors outside 1:1 meetings, suggesting that 1:1 meetings provide a unique and meaningful context for individualized, synchronous support. Overall, the results identify 1:1 meetings as a practical tool managers can use to promote direct reports' engagement and advance both meeting science and engagement literature.

title: Partner selection in project-based software development: the roles of performance, collaboration experience and network governance
authors: Yingchao Lan; Tingting Yan; Brett Massimino
affiliations: University of Nebraska-Lincoln , , ,; Texas Tech University , , ,; Virginia Commonwealth University , , ,
abstract: Purpose This study examines supplier selection in project-based software development, where buyers rely on external developers for specialized capabilities while facing substantial safeguarding risks. Adopting a network-governance perspective, we investigate how network overlap – the extent to which a publisher and developer share common partners – moderates the relationships between developer performance, prior collaboration experience and selection outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Using a longitudinal dataset from the electronic video game industry (7,583 products, 4,322 unique developers and 3,016 unique publishers, over 16 years), we model developer selection using a conditional logit framework. Findings Developers with stronger historical product performance, confidentiality performance and greater prior collaboration experience are more likely to be selected. Network overlap substitutes for prior collaboration experience while strengthening the association between confidentiality performance and selection likelihood, highlighting the contingent role of network governance in partner selection decisions in project-based software development. Originality/value This study advances supplier-selection research by examining observed partner selection in project-based software development. It integrates firm-level indicators, dyadic experience and network overlap, showing that network governance can substitute for prior collaboration while complementing confidentiality performance.

title: Who Benefits From Robots? Gender and Technology on the Shop Floor
authors: Ines Wagner; Virginia Doellgast
affiliations: ARENA Centre for European Studies University of Oslo Oslo Norway; ILR School Cornell University Ithaca New York USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The introduction of robots has produced uneven benefits for workers with different skills, occupations, and genders. We examine a qualitative case study of a Norwegian auto‐supply plant to ask why gender inequalities often persist on the shop floor, even in a gender‐progressive institutional context. The introduction of CNC machines in the plant made machining more like the female‐dominated assembly line in skill and strength demands, yet machining remained male‐dominated, with higher pay and greater investment in automation compared to the assembly line. The authors argue that persistent assumptions about economic value and gendered institutions and practices explain these unequal outcomes.

title: The Impacts of Host Culture Heterogeneity on Learning from Success Versus Failure in Foreign Direct Investments
authors: Yuping Zeng; Sangcheol Song; Soonkyoo Choe
affiliations: Southern Illinois University Edwardsville; Saint Joseph's University; Yonsei University
abstract: Abstract This study examines the differentiated influences of host culture heterogeneity on the learning outcomes of multinational enterprises' (MNEs) success and failure experiences in foreign direct investments (FDI). We posit that host culture heterogeneity among prior successful FDIs reduces the beneficial effect of an MNE's success experience on a subsequent FDI, particularly when the cultural differences between the subsequent FDI and the MNE's prior successes are significant. In contrast, host culture heterogeneity among prior failed FDIs enhances the learning benefits of failure experience, and this effect is more pronounced when the subsequent FDI is culturally distant from the prior failures. Using FDI data of South Korean MNEs between 1990 and 2016, we find support for our hypotheses, demonstrating that host culture heterogeneity has divergent impacts on the learning outcomes of MNEs' success versus failure FDI experiences. This study enhances our understanding of the conditions under which host culture heterogeneity may weaken or strengthen the learning benefits of an MNE's FDI experience.

title: Unethical Leadership and Employee Creative Unethicality—Do Dark Personalities Matter?
authors: Janja Annabel Tardios; Farhad Uddin Ahmed; Md Imtiaz Mostafiz; Puteh Noraihan A. Rahman; Shlomo Y. Tarba; Kumud Wijayaratna; Hakeem A. Owolabi
affiliations: Brunel Business School, Brunel University London Uxbridge UK; School of Business, Maynooth University Maynooth Ireland; University of Leicester School of Business, University of Leicester Leicester UK; Miyan Research Institute, International University of Business Agriculture and Technology (IUBAT) Dhaka Bangladesh; School of Liberal Studies (CITRA‐UKM), Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) Bangi Malaysia; Birmingham Business School, University of Birmingham Birmingham UK; Greater Manchester Business School, University of Bolton Bolton UK
abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that employee creativity may also be unethical; however, our understanding of such behaviour is limited. Existing literature suggests that certain leadership behaviours foster creativity; hence, employee creative unethicality may be similarly underpinned by unethical leadership—that is, leadership that rejects accepted norms. Building on the focus‐strand logic of self‐regulation theory, we argue that the degree of unethical leadership has an inverted U‐shaped relationship with employee creative unethicality, and that this relationship is conditional on employee Dark Triad personality traits. A time‐lagged survey of 468 employees from 26 firms in Bangladesh, India and Malaysia confirms the hypothesized inverted U‐shaped effect and finds that this relationship is positively moderated by employee Machiavellianism and psychopathy. The findings contribute to understanding when creative unethicality escalates within organizations by showing that unethical leadership does not invariably translate into employee creative unethicality. Under high unethical leadership, employees guided by self‐regulation may instead pursue more ethical solutions. However, when employees possess Machiavellian or psychopathic traits, their self‐regulatory tendencies are compromised, thereby increasing the likelihood of creative unethicality under unethical leadership.

title: Government‐funded experimentation: How startups use R&D contracts to resolve uncertainty
authors: Larisa Cioaca
affiliations: Freeman School of Business Tulane University New Orleans Louisiana USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Startups use experimentation to reduce technological and market uncertainty, but experimentation is costly and unevenly funded. This paper examines how government‐funded experimentation relates to subsequent performance among high‐tech startups that receive federal awards. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups between 2001 and 2018, I distinguish between technology experimentation, measured by the value of R&D contracts, and market experimentation, measured by the number of agencies awarding the R&D contracts. Market experimentation is positively associated with subsequent employment, sales, and acquisition, while technology experimentation shows weaker associations with these outcomes. The findings are consistent with startups using information from multiple government buyers to learn about market opportunities and improve subsequent performance. Managerial Summary High‐tech startups need to test both whether their technology works and where demand exists, but venture capital often leaves this experimentation unfunded. Using data on $32 billion in US government R&D contracts awarded to high‐tech startups from 2001 to 2018, this paper shows that startups funded by more government agencies subsequently have higher employment and sales and are more likely to be acquired. Larger R&D contract amounts have less consistent relationships with these outcomes. For managers, the findings suggest considering what different government customers can help the firm learn. For policymakers, they suggest that the diversity of a startup's public customer base is a vital margin to consider alongside the overall size of its R&D awards.

title: Human Capital as a Driver of Automation: Theory and Evidence From China's College Expansion
authors: Jianying Chen; Qichun He; Kai Li
affiliations: China Economics and Management Academy Central University of Finance and Economics Beijing China; Tsinghua University PBC School of Finance Beijing China; Peking University HSBC Business School Shenzhen China
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how human capital shapes both the level and direction of automation. We develop an endogenous Schumpeterian growth model in which skilled labor is allocated across production, horizontal automation of new tasks, and vertical upgrading of existing automated tasks. A positive skilled‐labor shock reallocates labor toward R&D and accelerates automation along both margins. Using China's 1999 college enrollment expansion as a natural experiment, we find that firms in skill‐intensive industries increased robot adoption significantly more after the reform, with a stronger effect on the horizontal than the vertical margin.

title: The old lady of economic history: 100 years of the Economic History Review
authors: Martina Cioni; Giovanni Federico; Michelangelo Vasta
affiliations: Department of Economics and Statistics University of Siena Siena Italy; Social Sciences Division New York University, Abu Dhabi, UAE and CEPR; Department of Economics and Statistics University of Siena, Siena, Italy, and CEPR
abstract: Abstract This article traces the evolution of the Economic History Review over its first century and places it within the broader transformation of economic history as a discipline. Drawing on a new database covering 2761 articles published in the journal between 1927 and 2025 by 2011 authors from 571 institutions in 50 countries, it analyses changes in editorial leadership, research topics, historical periods, geographical coverage, methods, authorship, and citation patterns. The findings suggest that the journal evolved from a predominantly UK outlet into one of the leading international journals in economic history. Over time, it converged towards the model of the major international field journals, with citation networks revealing a shift from stronger links with history to closer connections with economics. At the same time, however, the journal retained a distinctive profile, preserving a more historical orientation than the leading American journals. The article also documents a marked process of internationalization, reflected in both the geographical scope of published research and the growing presence of scholars from continental Europe. Finally, citation analysis shows that articles addressing long‐run and geographically comparative questions achieve the highest scholarly impact.

title: Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
authors: Robert M. Bushman; Sang Woo Sohn; Jianxin (Donny) Zhao
affiliations: University of North Carolina; City University of Hong Kong; Emory University
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs. We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.
